headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading-error pathways exist because Haystack has broad network/MCP access while oh-my-openagent reads project files and uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Haystack can call MCP servers and broad network egress, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if one agent’s outputs are fed into the other through shared MCP content or copied text. No direct shared channel is documented, so I choose medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Haystack output is routed into an MCP tool or hook consumed by oh-my-openagent, prompt-like text can steer execution.
IF oh-my-openagent ingests Haystack-generated content as instructions rather than data, injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Disable automatic tool-call execution on imported text.
Add provenance tags to MCP payloads.
Require a human approval step before executing instructions extracted from model output.
Restrict shared MCP endpoints to read-only data formats.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Haystack has broad network egress, and oh-my-openagent touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive local context can flow from oh-my-openagent into Haystack’s outbound requests. The pairwise path is plausible in default docs, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents run against the same workspace or credential store, oh-my-openagent can expose code and auth data to Haystack.
IF Haystack forwards retrieved context to external APIs, local project material can leave the machine.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate workspaces.
Remove provider auth data from any shared directory.
Disable network egress for Haystack when handling sensitive projects.
Rotate credentials before co-running the pair.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem and network sandboxing.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Haystack can use MCP servers and broad network egress, while oh-my-openagent supports multiple instances, subprocesses, and full-permissions mode. Overlapping write and execution surfaces make concurrent modification conflicts likely if they target the same repo or config files. Because locking is not documented, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or config path, concurrent writes can race.
IF oh-my-openagent runs in full-permissions mode while Haystack invokes MCP tools, shared mutable state can be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize access with a manual lock file.
Avoid running multiple oh-my-openagent instances on the same project.
Pause one agent before the other edits files.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Haystack is a search/RAG agent, so its outputs are likely to be treated as retrieved facts, while oh-my-openagent includes team_send_message and task-creation APIs that can act on those outputs. If Haystack’s retrieved content is forwarded without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. The action-taking surface makes high appropriate.
conditions: IF Haystack-generated retrievals are used as authoritative inputs to team_send_message or task creation, mistakes can propagate.
IF oh-my-openagent executes tasks based on unverified Haystack results, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require citation checks before task creation.
Insert a human review step for any action derived from Haystack output.
Limit team_send_message to summaries, not commands.
Mark retrieved facts as untrusted until verified.
requires-engineering: add automated verification against source documents.

E_compliance.rationale: Haystack is documented as touching anonymous usage statistics, while oh-my-openagent touches anonymous telemetry, installation identifiers, project code, session history, and provider authentication data. The pair creates a compliance mismatch risk around logging and retention if the same project data is processed by both, but no specific residency or regulated-data violation is documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF the same project data is processed by both agents, their telemetry and session-history retention policies must align.
IF provider authentication data is stored alongside project code, retention and access controls become compliance-relevant.
mitigations: Review both agents’ retention settings.
Exclude regulated data from shared runs.
Delete session history after each task.
Separate telemetry from project workspaces.
requires-engineering: document and enforce a common data-handling policy.
